problem:
$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}-1, & x\in [-2,0] \\ 2, & x\in (0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{1}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{\pi (2n-1)}sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.At $x=1,$ we have

$$
sin\,(\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{2})={{field-1}}.
$$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Value of an Infinite Sum Using Fourier Series
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070509/assets/1da7fe97b22b7a72b4253abfb180ce5f294fa945450879d8cb857ee1470edbf3.png)
Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. The Fourier series of the $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin((2n-1)x).
$$

Use this Fourier series to find the sum of the series

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}.
$$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we notice that at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we have

$$
\sin\left((2n-1)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}+n\pi\right) = (-1)^{n+1}.
$$

So, substituting $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ into the given Fourier series gives

$$
f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin\left((2n-1)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)
= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)}(-1)^{n+1}.
$$

Next, since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ the Fourier series converges to $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in [0,\pi),$ we have

$$
f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{\pi (2n-1)}(-1)^{n+1} \\ \frac{\pi }{4} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}.
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}, & x\in [-\pi ,0] \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x+1, & x\in (0,\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
f\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2})+1=2.
$$
